query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, conformal, high‐thermal‐conductivity diffusion barrier coating (for example, a Mo- or high-entropy alloy–based coating) uniformly onto the tungsten surfaces of a W–Cu composite will suppress phase separation and interfacial void formation during high heat flux and irradiation, thereby improving the overall thermal conductivity of the composite compared to the untreated state.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite material containing either discrete tungsten particles or an interconnected network of tungsten ligaments dispersed within a copper matrix that, in its untreated form, experiences phase separation at the W/Cu interfaces and forms interfacial voids under service conditions.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin (e.g., on the order of 100–200 nm), uniform, high-thermal-conductivity diffusion barrier coating (e.g., using magnetron sputtering of Mo or a refractory high-entropy alloy formulation) onto all exposed tungsten surfaces prior to composite consolidation.
generation.conditions: The treated composite is intended for joint regions in W-based plasma-facing components interfacing with Cu-based cooling systems. Tests would simulate the relevant high heat flux (e.g., 10–20 MW/m² steady/transient loads) and irradiation conditions (e.g., neutron or high-energy ion irradiation at temperatures in the range of 180–350 °C) encountered in fusion reactor applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A deliberately engineered, nanometer-scale interfacial layer between W and Cu that acts as a graded or diffusion barrier, preventing or mitigating interdiffusion that leads to phase separation and the nucleation of voids.
generation.mechanism: The applied coating reduces interfacial energy and suppresses interdiffusion between tungsten and copper during thermal cycling and irradiation exposure. This barrier mitigates the formation of intermetallic or void phases by relaxing local stresses (including those arising from thermal expansion mismatches) and promoting a continuous, graded transition at the interface, which supports more efficient phonon and electron transport.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated composite, the coated sample is expected to exhibit a more stable, homogeneous interface without voids or phase‐segregated regions, leading to an increased effective thermal conductivity under service conditions.
generation.baseline: An untreated W–Cu composite that exhibits detrimental phase separation and interfacial void formation under high heat flux and irradiation, resulting in reduced thermal conductivity and reliability in the joint regions of plasma-facing and cooling components.
generation.boundary: The intervention is applicable in systems where the thickness of the coating is optimized to maintain high thermal conduction and chemical compatibility between W and Cu. The approach is expected to be effective within the operating temperature range (roughly 180–350 °C) and under irradiation conditions typical of fusion reactor environments, but its effectiveness may be limited if the coating degrades under extreme radiation doses or if the coating thickness is not properly controlled.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the optimal composition/thickness of the coating, its long-term stability under prolonged irradiation, and potential changes in mechanical properties (e.g., ductility or adhesion) of the interface during cyclic thermal exposures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set receiving the proposed diffusion barrier coating on tungsten surfaces via magnetron sputtering, and a control set left untreated. Subject both sets to simulated service conditions that mimic high heat flux and irradiation (using, for example, ion irradiation and thermal cycling within the 180–350 °C range). Characterize the microstructure with electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to assess void formation and phase separation, and measure the thermal conductivity (using laser flash analysis or another appropriate method) both before and after exposure.
measurements: Interfacial microstructure (void density, phase homogeneity) by SEM/TEM.
Thermal conductivity of the composite before and after thermal/irradiation treatment.
Adhesion strength of the coating via micro/nanoindentation or scratch testing.
Diffusion profiles at the interface (using EDS line scans) to confirm suppression of interdiffusion.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples show no statistically significant reduction in interfacial void formation and phase segregation compared to the untreated composites, and if their thermal conductivity is not measurably improved under identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions, then the intervention does not achieve the intended performance improvement and the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Based on the morphological characteristics of the microstructure at the interface between HEA particles and matrix alloy, a two-layer structure was formed in the investigated AMCs, in which Layer I had only one phase and Layer II had two phases. Based on Figure 7 and Figure 11, Layer I corresponded to a Ni-poor region, while Layer II corresponded to a Ni-rich region. A reaction product was detected at the interface by TEM in the FSPed HEA/5083 composite [], but only the HEA particle and the matrix alloys could be detected based by XRD in this research. This suggested that these phases located in the shell zone maintained the BCC-type or FCC-type lattice structure, in which the aluminum content changed greatly but the atomic ratio of Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni alloying elements almost maintained equality. The crystal structure of the AlCoCrFeNi HEA alloys depended on the aluminum content due to the lattice distortion. Hence, the change in XRD Bragg peaks intensity of the AMCs before and after solution heat treatment indicated that the phases in the shell should still be Al-based solid solution.

AbstractIn this study, an effective way of applying Ti/Ni deposited coating to the surface of diamond single crystal particles by magnetron sputtering was proposed and novel high-entropy alloy (HEA)/diamond composites were prepared by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The results show that the interfacial bonding state of the coated diamond composite is obviously better than that of the uncoated diamond composite. Corresponding mechanical properties such as hardness, density, transverse fracture strength and friction properties of the coated diamond composite were also found to be better than those of the uncoated diamond composite. The effects of interface structure and defects on the mechanical properties of HEA/diamond composites were investigated. The research directions for further improving the structure and properties of high-entropy alloy/diamond composites were proposed. Keywords: high-entropy alloy, diamond, coating, interface, mechanical properties
